a: This is the book of the story of Tobit
t: "The book of the words of Tobit"
p: The Greek title is "book of words": a family story told as a record, the way prophets' books open.
b: The Greek biblos logōn means "book of words" or "book of the story." Prophetic books open the same way ("The words of Amos," Amos 1:1; "The words of Jeremiah," Jeremiah 1:1), and so does the Story of Ahiqar, a story the book knows, whose old Aramaic copy is titled "the words of Ahiqar" (see 1:21). The name Tobit probably comes from the Hebrew tov, "good": Tobi, "my good," short for Tobiah, "the LORD is my good." His son Tobias bears the full form. The names fit a story about God's goodness to a good man.
orig: ΒΙΒΛΟΣ λόγων Τωβεὶθ (biblos logōn Tōbeith), 'book of the words of Tobit'

a: from the tribe of Naphtali
t: A man of the lost northern tribes
p: Tobit belongs to Naphtali, one of the ten northern tribes that Assyria carried away.
b: Naphtali lived west of the Sea of Galilee. Its land was among the first taken by Assyria: "all the land of Naphtali" went into exile under Tiglath-pileser III in 732 BC (2 Kings 15:29), ten years before Samaria fell. By the time Tobit was written, Jews spoke of the ten tribes as scattered or lost. The book gives one of them a face and a family, and it ends with a hope that all the exiles will be gathered again (13:5; 14:5–7). For its first readers, Jews living far from the land, the point was plain: a faithful life is possible in exile, and God has not forgotten even the northern tribes.

a: Shalmaneser
p: The Greek has Enemessar, almost certainly a garbled form of Shalmaneser, the king who besieged Samaria.
b: Both Greek texts call the king Enemessaros. No Assyrian king had that name, and nearly all scholars take it as a corrupt form of Shalmaneser (Assyrian Shulmanu-asharedu). Shalmaneser V (727–722 BC) besieged Samaria (2 Kings 17:3–6; 2 Kings 18:9–11), and his successor Sargon II claimed its capture. The Latin Vulgate has "Salmanasar." The Plain uses the familiar name, as most English Bibles do. Note that the Bible puts Naphtali's exile earlier, under Tiglath-pileser (2 Kings 15:29): the book's history is loose, a point taken up at 1:15.
orig: Ἐνεμεσσάρου (Enemessarou)

a: on the south side of Kedesh of Naphtali
p: The Greek says "on the right of Kedesh": facing east, as ancient people did, the right hand is south.
b: Israelites gave directions facing the sunrise, so "right" is south and "left" north; the Greek here says "to the right of Kedesh" and "to the left of Phogor." Kedesh of Naphtali was a city of refuge in upper Galilee (Joshua 20:7) and Barak's hometown (Judges 4:6), taken by Tiglath-pileser (2 Kings 15:29). Thisbe is otherwise unknown; Elijah "the Tishbite" (1 Kings 17:1) may be named for a different Tishbe. "Asser" may be Hazor, written Asōr in Greek, or the tribe of Asher. Phogor has not been identified.
orig: ἐκ δεξιῶν Κυδιὼς (ek dexiōn Kydiōs), 'on the right of Kedesh'

a: All the days of my life I, Tobit, have walked in the ways of truth
p: From 1:3 to 3:6 Tobit speaks as "I"; at 3:7 a narrator takes over.
b: The first part of the book is a memoir in the first person, like Nehemiah's memoir (Nehemiah 1–7) or the Aramaic Story of Ahiqar, in which the wise man tells of his own fall and rescue. At 3:7 the voice changes to "he" and "she" so that Sarah's story can run beside Tobit's. Tobit opens by listing his virtues: truth, right deeds and alms. Readers have argued whether the book means us to admire him without reserve, or to notice that a man so sure of his own goodness will soon be blind, poor, and quick to accuse his wife (2:13–14).

a: alms
p: Greek eleēmosynē, "mercy" shown to the poor. It is Tobit's favorite word for a faithful life.
b: Eleēmosynē comes from eleos, "mercy," and the English "alms" comes from it through Latin. It means mercy put into action, above all gifts of food, clothing, money or burial to people in need. Tobit uses it more than any other book of the Greek Old Testament. The Plain says "alms" for a person's acts and "mercy" when it is God's (3:2). In the Septuagint the word often stands for the Hebrew tsedaqah, "righteousness," which by Tobit's time had come to mean charity (compare Daniel 4:27). Tobit pairs the two: "truth" and "right deeds" here, "alms" and "right deeds" in Anna's taunt (2:14).
orig: ἐλεημοσύνας πολλὰς ἐποίησα (eleēmosynas pollas epoiēsa), 'I did many alms'

a: broke away from the house of my ancestor David and from Jerusalem
p: Tobit looks back to the northern tribes' break with David's line (1 Kings 12).
b: When Solomon's son Rehoboam refused to lighten the people's load, the northern tribes cried, "To your tents, Israel!" and made Jeroboam king (1 Kings 12:16–20). Tobit calls David "my father," meaning the founder of the royal house his people once served, not his own ancestor; he is from Naphtali, not Judah. His point is that Naphtali's break was not only political but religious: it cut the tribe off from the one temple. Vaticanus has a shorter wording (see the variant).

a: where all Israel's tribes were to offer sacrifice
p: Tobit holds the rule of Deuteronomy: sacrifice belongs at one chosen place, Jerusalem.
b: Agrees: Deuteronomy commands Israel to bring offerings only to "the place the LORD your God will choose" (Deuteronomy 12:5, 13–14), and Kings names it Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:36). Tobit's praise of the temple and his blame of the northern shrines match the judgment of Kings on Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:30; 2 Kings 17:21–23). Goes beyond: the line about a temple built "for every generation to come" sounds strange from a man who is supposed to live before 722 BC, since it was destroyed in 586; first readers around 200 BC knew a rebuilt temple, and 14:5 looks ahead to a still more glorious one.

a: the calf that Jeroboam king of Israel had made in Dan
p: Jeroboam set up two gold calves, at Bethel and Dan. Naphtali lived near Dan, so Tobit names that one.
b: Kings tells how Jeroboam, afraid that pilgrims to Jerusalem would turn back to David's house, made two gold calves: "He placed one calf in Bethel, and the other he put in Dan" (1 Kings 12:29). Dan lay at the northern edge of Naphtali's land, so it was Tobit's tribe's local shrine. Sinaiticus speaks of sacrifices "on all the mountains of Galilee," the high places the prophets condemned. Vaticanus instead has "Baal the heifer," with the feminine article (see the variant).

a: as the everlasting law written for all Israel commands
p: Tobit keeps the three pilgrim festivals and all the tithes, alone among his tribe.
b: The law tells every Israelite male to appear before the LORD three times a year "at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, at the Feast of Weeks and at the Feast of Booths" (Deuteronomy 16:16). Tobit pictures himself as the one northerner who still obeyed, like the faithful remnant of 1 Kings 19:18. Agrees with the law in substance. Goes beyond it in detail: Tobit combines the tithe laws of Numbers and Deuteronomy into three separate tithes, as later Jewish teachers did (see 1:7–8).

a: the second tenth
p: Tobit gives three tithes: one to the Levites, one eaten in Jerusalem, and one for the poor every third year.
b: The law has several tithe rules. A tenth goes to the Levites (Numbers 18:21–24); a tenth is eaten by the family "before the LORD" at the sanctuary, and may be turned into money for the journey (Deuteronomy 14:22–26); and every third year a tithe is stored in the towns for "the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow" (Deuteronomy 14:28–29; Deuteronomy 26:12). Later Jews read these as three different tithes, called in the Mishnah the first tithe, the second tithe and the poor tithe. Tobit 1:6–8 is one of the oldest witnesses to that reading. Jubilees 32:10–15 knows the second tithe, eaten each year before the LORD, and Josephus (Antiquities 4.240) knows all three, including a third tithe for the needy.

a: For six years out of seven
p: The Greek says only "I tithed the second tenth in money of the six years". The meaning is uncertain.
b: The phrase tōn hex etōn, "of the six years," seems to refer to the seven-year cycle that ends with the year of release (Deuteronomy 15:1), when there was no harvest to tithe. Others think it means "for six years" in a row. Vaticanus has a simpler text: "the second tenth I sold, and went and spent it in Jerusalem." The Plain gives the most likely sense.
orig: ἀπεδεκάτιζον ἀργυρίῳ τῶν ἓξ ἐτῶν (apedekatizon argyriō tōn hex etōn)

a: converts who had joined the Israelites
p: The Greek prosēlytos first meant a foreigner living in Israel; by Tobit's time it meant a convert.
b: The Septuagint used prosēlytos for the Hebrew ger, the "foreigner who lives among you" whom the law protects (Exodus 22:21; Deuteronomy 14:29). In Jewish Greek of the last centuries BC it came to mean a Gentile who had joined the Jewish people, as in Matthew 23:15 and Acts 2:10. Tobit's wording, "who had joined the Israelites," points to that newer sense, so the Plain says "converts."
orig: προσηλύτοις τοῖς προσκειμένοις (prosēlytois tois proskeimenois)

a: Deborah, the mother of our forefather Ananiel
p: Sinaiticus makes Deborah the mother of Ananiel, Tobit's grandfather; Vaticanus calls her his father's mother.
b: By 1:1, Ananiel is Tobit's grandfather, so "the mother of Ananiel our father" in Sinaiticus makes Deborah his great-grandmother, with "father" meaning forefather. Vaticanus says "my father's mother." Either way, an orphan is raised in the law by a woman of the family. The Bible honors a mother's teaching (Proverbs 1:8; Proverbs 31:1), and the New Testament praises Timothy's grandmother Lois and mother Eunice for the same thing (2 Timothy 1:5).

a: ate the food of the Gentiles
p: Like Daniel and Judith, Tobit refuses Gentile food. The law of Moses bans unclean animals, not Gentile bread as such.
b: Daniel "resolved not to defile himself" with the king's food (Daniel 1:8), Judith brings her own food into the Assyrian camp (Judith 12:1–4), and the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6–7 die rather than eat pork. Goes beyond: the law forbids unclean animals and blood (Leviticus 11; Leviticus 17:10–14), but says nothing against bread made by Gentiles. Jews of the Persian and Greek periods widened the rule, because food in a Gentile house could have been offered to idols or be impure. Peter's "I have never eaten anything common and unclean" (Acts 10:14) and the complaint that he ate with Gentiles (Acts 11:3) show the same custom.

a: favor and good standing
p: The Greek says God gave Tobit charis and morphē, "grace and form": favor and a good appearance.
b: Morphē means outward form; here it is the good impression Tobit made at court. Joseph found favor in Potiphar's eyes and the jailer's (Genesis 39:4, 21), Daniel with the chief official (Daniel 1:9), and Esther with the king (Esther 2:17). Tobit stands in this line of Jews who serve foreign kings well without giving up their faith.
orig: χάριν καὶ μορφὴν (charin kai morphēn)

a: ten talents in all
p: A talent was about 30 kilograms of silver. Ten talents was enough to make a family rich.
b: The talent was the largest ancient weight, roughly 30 to 34 kilograms (66 to 75 pounds). Ten talents of silver is a fortune, many lifetimes of a laborer's pay (compare the drachma a day in 5:15). Tobit leaves it "in the keeping" of a kinsman: the Greek paratithēmi is the word for a trust deposit, which the law governs in Exodus 22:7–13. The money is what sends Tobias on his journey.

a: Media
t: Media, where the exiles were sent
p: Media, in the mountains of northwestern Iran, was one of the places where Israel was exiled.
b: Kings says the king of Assyria settled the exiles "in Halah, by the Habor River of Gozan, and in the towns of Media" (2 Kings 17:6). Media's two cities in the story are Ecbatana, its capital (modern Hamadan), and Rages (Rhagae, near modern Tehran). In Tobit's day Media was under Assyria only loosely; later it became part of the Persian empire, and Ecbatana a royal residence (Ezra 6:2).

a: his son Sennacherib became king in his place
p: Sennacherib was Sargon II's son, not Shalmaneser's. The book skips a king and compresses decades.
b: Assyrian records give the order Tiglath-pileser III (745–727 BC), Shalmaneser V (727–722), Sargon II (722–705), Sennacherib (705–681), Esarhaddon (681–669). Tobit leaves out Sargon and makes Sennacherib Shalmaneser's son. The Bible names Sargon only once (Isaiah 20:1). Most scholars take such slips as signs that the book was written centuries later, as a story set in the past; the book's own canon page discusses how churches that read Tobit as Scripture answer this. Vaticanus names the king "Acheriel" here (see the variant).

a: The roads into Media were cut off
p: The Greek says the roads of Media "stood apart" or "revolted": travel there became unsafe.
b: The verb apestēsan is the one used of Naphtali "breaking away" in 1:4. Here it probably means that Media rebelled or that its roads became unsafe. Vaticanus says "his roads became unsettled." Sennacherib's reign did see revolts in the east, but the book gives no details.
orig: αἱ ὁδοὶ τῆς Μηδείας ἀπέστησαν (hai hodoi tēs Mēdeias apestēsan)

a: I gave my bread to people who were hungry and clothing to people who had none
t: Feeding the hungry, clothing the naked
p: Tobit's works are the prophets' and Jesus' list: bread for the hungry, clothes for the naked.
b: Isaiah calls the true fast sharing "your bread with the hungry" and covering the naked (Isaiah 58:7), Ezekiel names the same deeds as marks of the righteous man (Ezekiel 18:7, 16), and Job claims them (Job 31:17–20). Jesus makes them the test at the judgment (Matthew 25:35–36). Tobit gives the same advice to his son in 4:16.

a: I buried him
p: The 66 books honor burial; Tobit makes it a central good work. Christians later counted it a work of mercy.
b: Agrees: in the Bible a body left unburied is a curse (Deuteronomy 28:26; Jeremiah 16:4; Psalm 79:2–3), and burying the dead is praised: the men of Jabesh-gilead bury Saul (1 Samuel 31:11–13), and David blesses them for it (2 Samuel 2:5). Goes beyond: no book of the 66 makes burial of strangers a standing duty in the way Tobit does. Christian writers took it from Tobit: Thomas Aquinas counts "to bury the dead" among the seven bodily works of mercy, the six of Matthew 25 with this one added, and praises Tobias's example in his reply to the first objection (Summa II-II q.32 a.2, ad 1). The Catholic Catechism lists it today (Catechism 2447).
r: Deuteronomy 28:26; Jeremiah 16:4; Psalm 79:2–3; 1 Samuel 31:11–13; 2 Samuel 2:5; Matthew 25:35–36

a: thrown out behind the city wall of Nineveh
p: Ancient kings left rebels' bodies unburied as a warning. Greek tragedy has a sister who defies such a ban.
b: Assyrian royal inscriptions boast of piling up the corpses of enemies, and leaving a body exposed was a punishment that reached beyond death. The best-known ancient story of someone burying a body against a king's order is Sophocles' Antigone (about 441 BC), in which Antigone buries her brother and dies for it. Verdict: there is no sign that Tobit borrows from Antigone; both reflect a value shared across the ancient world, that the dead are owed burial. Tobit's motive is his own: the dead are his own people ("one of my own people").

a: when he fled from Judea
p: Kings tells of Sennacherib's failed attack on Jerusalem in 701 BC; Tobit adds his revenge in Nineveh.
b: When Sennacherib's officer mocked the God of Israel, Hezekiah prayed, and "the angel of the LORD" struck the Assyrian camp (2 Kings 19:4, 22, 35). Then "Sennacherib king of Assyria pulled up stakes and left. He went back home and stayed in Nineveh" (2 Kings 19:36). Tobit calls this the judgment of "the King of heaven" for his "blasphemies," the same charge Kings makes (2 Kings 19:6, 22). Goes beyond: the Bible says nothing of Sennacherib taking out his anger on Israelites in Nineveh; that is the book's own story.

a: the King of heaven
p: A title for God found in Daniel 4:37 and again in Tobit's song (13:7, 11).
b: Nebuchadnezzar ends his madness praising "the King of heaven" (Daniel 4:37). The title fits the exile: earthly kings like Sennacherib rule for a time, but the true king rules from heaven. Tobit uses it again in his song of praise (13:7, 11), and Matthew's "kingdom of heaven" grows from the same way of speaking.
orig: ὁ βασιλεὺς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ (ho basileus tou ouranou)

a: his two sons killed him and escaped to the mountains of Ararat
p: 2 Kings 19:37 records the same murder and flight to Ararat. History puts it twenty years after 701 BC, not forty days.
b: Kings says Sennacherib was killed by two of his sons while worshiping, and "They escaped to the land of Ararat, and his son Esarhaddon became king in his place" (2 Kings 19:37). Babylonian records confirm that Sennacherib was murdered in 681 BC and that Esarhaddon succeeded him. Agrees with Kings on the murder, Ararat (Urartu, in Armenia) and the heir. Differs on the timing: Tobit puts the murder within forty days of Sennacherib's anger (Vaticanus: fifty), while history and Kings leave twenty years between the retreat of 701 and the murder of 681.

a: Ahiqar
t: Ahiqar, the wise man of Assyria
p: Ahiqar is the hero of a famous Aramaic tale and book of sayings. Tobit makes him a Jew and his nephew.
b: The Story of Ahiqar tells of a wise scribe of Sennacherib and Esarhaddon who adopts his nephew Nadin, is betrayed by him, is saved, and ends with a collection of proverbs. The oldest copy is an Aramaic papyrus from the Jewish garrison at Elephantine in Egypt, from the 400s BC, and later versions survive in Syriac, Arabic, Armenian and other languages. A cuneiform tablet from Uruk, of the Seleucid period, lists a sage of Esarhaddon "whom the Arameans call Ahuqar." Tobit makes this famous figure his own kinsman, and returns to his story in 11:18 and 14:10. For first readers it was as if a modern story made a famous statesman the hero's nephew.

a: chief cupbearer, keeper of the signet ring, governor and treasurer
t: A Jew at a foreign court
p: Ahiqar holds the same posts as Joseph and Nehemiah: the king's cupbearer and holder of his seal.
b: Pharaoh gives Joseph his signet ring (Genesis 41:42), Nehemiah says, "I served as the king's cupbearer" (Nehemiah 1:11), and Mordecai receives the king's ring (Esther 8:2). Stories like these told diaspora Jews that they could rise high in a foreign empire and still help their people. The cupbearer tasted the king's wine and so had to be fully trusted. "Keeper of the signet ring" sealed the king's orders.

a: appointed him again
p: The Greek ek deuteras usually means "a second time"; the KJV reads "next unto him."
b: Ek deuteras most naturally means "again, for the second time": Esarhaddon kept his father's minister. The KJV, following Vaticanus, takes it as "next unto him," second in rank, as Joseph was second to Pharaoh (Genesis 41:43). Both fit the Ahiqar story, in which he served both kings.
orig: κατέστησεν αὐτὸν Σαχερδονὸς ἐκ δευτέρας (katestēsen auton Sacherdonos ek deuteras)

a: He was my nephew
p: The Greek exadelphos usually means "cousin," but 1:21 makes Ahiqar the son of Tobit's brother.
b: In later Greek exadelphos means a cousin; in some texts it means a nephew. Since 1:21 calls Ahiqar "my brother Anael's son," the Plain says "nephew." Family words in Tobit are loose: "brother" often means any fellow Israelite (5:10), and a wife can be called "sister" (5:21).
orig: ἐξάδελφός μου (exadelphos mou)

a: At our festival of Pentecost, the holy Feast of Weeks
p: One of the first places the Feast of Weeks is called Pentecost, "fiftieth": fifty days after Passover.
b: The law calls it the Feast of Weeks, counted seven weeks from the first sheaf (Leviticus 23:15–16; Deuteronomy 16:9–10). Greek-speaking Jews called it Pentēkostē, "the fiftieth (day)," as here and in 2 Maccabees 12:32, and so does the New Testament (Acts 2:1; 1 Corinthians 16:8). The law tells Israel to rejoice at this feast with "the Levite who lives in your towns, and the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow" (Deuteronomy 16:11), which is why Tobit sends for a poor man to share his dinner.

a: who remembers God with his whole heart
p: The Greek says only "who remembers with his whole heart"; Vaticanus adds "the Lord".
b: Sinaiticus leaves the object unstated, and the Plain supplies "God," as the sense requires (compare 1:12, "I remembered my God with all my soul"). Tobit wants a poor man who is also faithful. Jesus' advice is wider: "when you hold a feast, call in people who are poor, crippled, lame or blind" (Luke 14:13), with no test of piety.
orig: ὃς μέμνηται ἐν ὅλῃ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ (hos memnētai en holē kardia autou)

a: until the sun went down, when I would bury him
p: Burying the man in daylight would be seen. Tobit had already been hunted for this (1:19).
b: Tobit waits for sunset because burying Israelites had once cost him everything (1:19–20), and his neighbors' mockery in 2:8 shows the danger was real. The law also says a body must not be left overnight (Deuteronomy 21:23), so he buries the man the same evening. Touching a corpse made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11–13), which explains his washing in 2:5 and 2:9.

a: the prophet Amos
p: Tobit remembers Amos's warning that God would turn Israel's feasts into mourning: his own Pentecost has.
b: Amos 8:10 reads, in the Hebrew, that God will turn "your festivals into mourning and all your songs into a lament." Tobit's Greek agrees on "festivals into mourning," but Sinaiticus has "all your ways," probably a copying slip for "songs" (the two Greek words look alike), and Vaticanus has "all your merrymaking" (see the variant). Amos spoke at Bethel, the northern shrine (Amos 7:10–13), which is why Tobit says "against Bethel." It is one of the few places where Tobit quotes a prophet by name; the other is 14:4 (Nahum or Jonah).

a: He was already hunted to be killed for this very thing
p: Sinaiticus slips into "I was hunted" in the neighbors' mouths; the rest of the line has "he ran away".
b: The Greek of Sinaiticus has epezētēthēn, "I was sought," inside the neighbors' words, then "he ran away" and "he is burying." Most scholars treat "I" as a copyist's slip, since Tobit is telling the story in the first person. Vaticanus reads "He is no longer afraid of being killed for this." The Plain gives the sense of both.
orig: ἤδη γὰρ ἐπεζητήθην (ēdē gar epezētēthēn), 'for I was already sought'

a: white films
p: The Greek leukōmata is a medical word for white scars on the cornea.
b: Greek medical writers use leukōma for a white patch that clouds the clear front of the eye. Bird droppings in the eye could cause an infection that left such scars. The doctors' ointments make it worse, a detail that reminds readers of the woman whom many doctors had put "through a great deal," until she "had only gotten worse" (Mark 5:26). The healing in 11:11–13 will peel the films away, as 3:17 promises.
orig: λευκώματα (leukōmata)

a: Elymais
p: Elymais is the Greek name for Elam, east of Babylon. The name points to a writer of the Greek period.
b: Elam, the land around Susa in southwestern Iran (Isaiah 21:2; Daniel 8:2), was called Elymais by Greek writers after Alexander. 1 Maccabees 6:1 knows a rich temple there. Using that name for a place in the 600s BC is one of several signs that the book comes from the Hellenistic age, as is the Macedonian month name in 2:12.

a: Dystrus
p: Dystrus is a month of the Macedonian calendar, about February to March. Only Sinaiticus has it.
b: The Greek kingdoms that followed Alexander used Macedonian month names, and Jews in the Greek world matched them to their own months; Dystrus falls around Adar, the last month before the new year. The detail is missing in Vaticanus. It adds to the impression that the longer text was written or copied in the Greek period.

a: Has it been stolen?
t: Is Tobit a model or a warning?
p: Tobit wrongly accuses his wife. Readers disagree on how far the book wants us to admire him.
b: Tobit's suspicion has a basis in the law, which forbids profiting from stolen animals (Exodus 22:1–4). But he does not believe Anna's plain answer, and she turns his own virtues against him. Some readers see a flawless saint tested like Job. Many recent scholars read a gentler irony: a good man whose suffering has made him proud and harsh, and who must learn that his goodness does not earn God's favor; his prayer in 3:1–6 begins that change. Jerome's Latin (2:12–18) takes the first view and adds that God allowed the trial "as an example of patience, as of holy Job."

a: I turned red with anger at her
p: The Greek verb means "I blushed". It can mean shame or anger; the KJV has "I was abashed at her."
b: Prosērythriōn is literally "I went red toward her." The context, in which Tobit keeps insisting and Anna answers sharply, suggests anger. The KJV's "abashed" takes it as embarrassment. Either way the scene is a quarrel in a household under strain.
orig: προσηρυθρίων (prosērythriōn)

a: Where are your alms now?
p: Anna's words recall Job's wife: where has your goodness got you?
b: Job's wife asks, "Still holding on to your integrity? Curse God, and die" (Job 2:9). Anna does not tell Tobit to curse God, but she throws his good deeds back at him in the same way. The Greek Job's wife also complains that she must work as a servant to feed them (Septuagint Job 2:9), as Anna does here. The Vulgate makes the comparison with Job explicit.

a: Look, all this about you is known!
p: Anna's last words are unclear in Greek: either "your true nature is plain" or "see what your good deeds got you".
b: The Greek ide tauta meta sou gnōsta estin is literally "look, these things are known with you." It can mean that Tobit's real character is now exposed, or that everyone can see what his alms have done for him (blindness and poverty). Vaticanus has "everything about you is known." Either way she accuses him of hypocrisy, and the charge drives him to prayer.
orig: ἴδε ταῦτα μετὰ σοῦ γνωστά ἐστιν (ide tauta meta sou gnōsta estin)

a: with groans I began to pray
p: Tobit's prayer follows the pattern of the great prayers of the exile: God is just; we sinned; have mercy.
b: Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9 and Daniel 9 are long prayers that begin by declaring God righteous, confess the sins of the people and their fathers, admit that exile is deserved, and ask for mercy. Tobit's prayer is a short personal form of the same pattern. In the story the prayer also marks a turn: the man who listed his own good deeds now confesses his sins.

a: Every path you take is mercy and truth
p: Tobit's words echo Psalm 25:10. He uses eleēmosynē, his word for alms, for God's mercy.
b: Psalm 25:10 says, "Every path the LORD takes is loyal love and faithfulness." The Hebrew pair hesed and emet becomes "mercy and truth" in Greek. Tobit uses eleēmosynē, the same word as for his own alms (1:3): human almsgiving copies God's own mercy. The confession "you are righteous, Lord" also opens Psalm 119:137 and Daniel 9:7.
orig: πᾶσαι αἱ ὁδοί σου ἐλεημοσύνη καὶ ἀλήθεια (pasai hai hodoi sou eleēmosynē kai alētheia)

a: my unknowing wrongs
p: The Greek agnoēmata are sins done without knowing: the law's "unintentional sins."
b: Leviticus 4 and Numbers 15:22–29 set offerings for sins done unintentionally, and Hebrews 9:7 uses the same Greek word for the people's "sins of ignorance" that the high priest covered on the Day of Atonement. Tobit asks forgiveness for wrongs he may not know he did, as the psalmist does: "Clear me of faults I cannot see" (Psalm 19:12).
orig: τοῖς ἀγνοήμασίν μου (tois agnoēmasin mou)

a: or for those of my ancestors
p: Tobit confesses his ancestors' sins with his own, as Daniel and Nehemiah do.
b: Agrees: the law speaks of God visiting the fathers' guilt on later generations of those who hate him (Exodus 20:5), and the exile prayers confess the sins of the people and of their ancestors together (Daniel 9:16): Nehemiah prays, "I and my father's family have sinned" (Nehemiah 1:6). Ezekiel 18:20 insists that each person bears his own guilt. Tobit holds both together: he asks not to be punished for his ancestors' sins, but he confesses them as his people's sins, standing with them.

a: I sinned against you
p: Sinaiticus can be read "I sinned"; Vaticanus clearly means the ancestors: "which they sinned".
b: The Greek hēmarton can mean either "I sinned" or "they sinned". Vaticanus makes it "they": "(the sins) which they sinned before you", and goes on "for they disobeyed your commands". In Sinaiticus the next verse has the singular "and I disobeyed" (parēkousa), which supports "I sinned" here; a later corrector (ℵc.a) changed it to the plural "they disobeyed", Swete reports. The Plain follows Sinaiticus as first written, so Tobit confesses his own sin with his people's, as in the prayers of Daniel 9 and Nehemiah 1.
orig: ἥμαρτον ἐναντίον σου (hēmarton enantion sou)

a: You made us a proverb, a thing people gossip about and mock
p: Tobit sees the exile as the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28 coming true.
b: Deuteronomy warns that if Israel breaks the covenant, "You will become a sight that shocks people, an example in their sayings and a target of their jokes, among all the peoples the LORD drives you to" (Deuteronomy 28:37). Solomon hears the same warning about the temple (1 Kings 9:7). Tobit's prayer accepts this reading of history: the exile is not bad luck but judgment, and so the way back is repentance.

a: Give the order to take my spirit from me
p: Moses, Elijah, Jonah and Job asked God to let them die. Tobit and Sarah do the same on the same day.
b: Moses (Numbers 11:15), Elijah (1 Kings 19:4), Jonah (Jonah 4:3) and Job (Job 6:8–9) all ask God to take their lives. Agrees: the Bible records such prayers honestly and never treats them as unbelief; God answers each one by providing, not by granting death. Tobit asks God to do it, not to take his own life, and the story answers him the same way: with healing, a journey and a wedding.

a: turn back into earth
p: Tobit echoes God's word to Adam: you are dust, and to dust you will return.
b: Genesis 3:19 says humans return to the ground they came from, and Ecclesiastes 12:7 that the dust returns to the earth and the spirit to God who gave it. Tobit's prayer has both parts: his spirit is "taken" and his body becomes earth.

a: the everlasting place
p: Probably the grave or the world of the dead, as in Ecclesiastes' "eternal home". Later readers heard heaven.
b: Ecclesiastes calls the grave a person's "eternal home" (Ecclesiastes 12:5), and Tobit's "everlasting place" probably means the same: the realm of the dead from which no one returns. The book elsewhere speaks of Hades (3:10; 4:19; 13:2). Later Jewish and Christian readers, who believed in reward after death, could hear a hope of rest with God; the Vulgate has "command my spirit to be received in peace." The Greek alone does not settle what Tobit expected.
orig: εἰς τὸν τόπον τὸν αἰώνιον (eis ton topon ton aiōnion)

a: That same day
p: The story jumps 450 miles to Ecbatana. Two people far apart pray for death on the same day, and both are heard.
b: The narrator now speaks of Tobit as "he" and starts a second story. The repeated "that same day," "at that moment" (3:11, 3:16, 3:17) ties the two together: each is insulted, each goes to a high or open place, each prays for death, and one angel is sent to answer both. Readers are meant to see what the characters cannot: God is weaving two lives together. Ecbatana (modern Hamadan) was the old Median capital (Ezra 6:2).

a: Asmodeus, the evil demon
p: The demon's name probably comes from Iranian aēšma-daēva, "demon of wrath." Later Jews made him king of demons.
b: Most scholars trace Asmodaios to the Avestan aēšma-daēva (Avestan is the language of the Zoroastrian scriptures), the demon of wrath in Zoroastrian texts; some suggest a Hebrew root meaning "to destroy." In the Babylonian Talmud Ashmedai is king of the demons, tricked by Solomon into helping build the temple (Gittin 68a–b), and in the Testament of Solomon Asmodeus confesses that he plots against newlyweds. The 66 books name no demon like this; they speak of Satan and of unnamed unclean spirits. On the demon's desire for Sarah, see 6:15.
orig: Ἀσμοδαῖος τὸ δαιμόνιον τὸ πονηρὸν (Asmodaios to daimonion to ponēron)

a: before he could sleep with her as husbands do
p: None of the seven marriages was consummated, so Sarah is still a virgin (3:14).
b: The Greek says the demon killed them "before they had been with her, as is appointed for wives." Each husband died on the wedding night (6:14). This matters for the plot: Sarah is still a virgin and still her father's heir. It also sets up the danger Tobias faces, and the Sadducees' puzzle about a woman married to seven brothers (Mark 12:20–23) may borrow the same motif. The closest parallel in the 66 books is Tamar: after two of Judah's sons die as her husbands, Judah keeps his youngest from her, thinking, "Or he too will die, like his brothers" (Genesis 38:11). Tobias has the same fear (6:14–15).

a: wanting to hang herself
p: Sarah thinks of hanging herself and decides against it for her father's sake. She prays instead.
b: Agrees: the 66 books tell of a few suicides (Saul, 1 Samuel 31:4; Ahithophel, 2 Samuel 17:23; Judas, Matthew 27:5) without approving any. Sarah's reasoning is about her father's shame and grief, and then she brings her despair to God. The scene is one of the few in ancient Jewish literature to show someone choosing against suicide, and it has comforted readers in despair: she is honest about wanting to die, and she prays.

a: down to Hades in sorrow
p: Sarah's words echo Jacob's fear that losing his son would bring him to Sheol in grief.
b: Jacob says, "you will send me down to Sheol, gray-haired and grieving" (Genesis 42:38; compare Genesis 37:35; Genesis 44:29–31). The Septuagint renders Sheol by Hadēs, the Greek name for the world of the dead, and Tobit follows it. Tobias uses nearly the same words of his parents in 6:15.
orig: εἰς ᾅδου (eis hadou)

a: spread out her hands toward the window
p: Like Daniel, Sarah prays at a window, with hands spread out: the posture of prayer.
b: Daniel prays three times a day at windows opened "toward Jerusalem" (Daniel 6:10), as Solomon asked exiles to pray toward the city and the temple (1 Kings 8:44, 48). Spreading the hands was the ancient posture of prayer (Exodus 9:29; 1 Kings 8:22; Psalm 143:6), later seen in early Christian art of figures praying with raised hands.

a: Blessed are you, merciful God
p: Sarah's prayer opens with the blessing formula later fixed in Jewish prayer: "Blessed are you, Lord."
b: The Hebrew barukh attah, "blessed are you," begins David's prayer in 1 Chronicles 29:10 and Psalm 119:12. In later Judaism nearly every prayer begins this way. Tobit's prayers (3:11; 8:5, 15; 11:14; 13:1) are among the earliest examples of the form outside the Hebrew Bible, and the first Christians used it too (Ephesians 1:3; 1 Peter 1:3).

a: no close kinsman or relative for whom I should keep myself as a wife
p: An only daughter who inherits was to marry within her father's tribe. Sarah sees no kinsman left.
b: When Zelophehad's daughters inherited his land, the law ruled: "Any daughter who inherits land in an Israelite tribe must marry a man from a clan of her father's tribe" (Numbers 36:8). Sarah, an only child and heir, expects to marry a kinsman, but she knows of none. The reader already knows of one: Tobias (3:17; 6:12). The book stretches the Numbers rule into a wider ideal of marrying kin, which Tobit preaches in 4:12.

a: Raphael was sent
p: Raphael's name means "God heals." The 66 books name only two angels, Michael and Gabriel.
b: Raphael is Hebrew Repha'el, "God heals," exactly his task here. The readers know who he is; Tobit and Tobias will not know until 12:15, where he calls himself one of seven angels who stand before God. Goes beyond: in the 66 books only Gabriel (Daniel 8:16; Luke 1:19) and Michael (Daniel 10:13; Jude 9; Revelation 12:7) are named. 1 Enoch also names Raphael among the holy angels (1 Enoch 20:3) and has him bind Azazel (1 Enoch 10:4), much as he binds Asmodeus in Tobit 8:3. On whether Christians should honor angels by names outside the 66, see the card at 1 Enoch 20.
r: Daniel 8:16; Daniel 10:13; Luke 1:19; Jude 9; 12:15; 1 Enoch 20:3; 1 Enoch 10:4

a: to receive her as his inheritance
p: The Greek verb is "inherit": Tobias has the next right to Sarah, as next of kin.
b: Klēronomēsai is the ordinary verb for inheriting property. The book speaks of Tobias "inheriting" Sarah (3:17; 6:12–13) because marriage to an heiress and the right to the family's estate went together for the nearest kinsman, much as Boaz's right to Ruth went with Naomi's field (Ruth 4:5). The language sounds cold today, but in the story it guards Sarah: she belongs to a family that must protect her.
orig: κληρονομῆσαι αὐτὴν (klēronomēsai autēn)

a: Look, I have asked for death
p: Thinking his prayer for death will be answered, Tobit gives his son a farewell charge.
b: Chapter 4 is a testament, the farewell teaching of a dying father, like Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49), Moses' last speeches (Deuteronomy 31–33) and David's charge to Solomon (1 Kings 2:1–9). Later Jewish books such as the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs are built entirely in this form. The irony is that Tobit does not die: he lives to see his son come home and gives a second testament in chapter 14. Readers who know the ending hear chapter 4 as the book's teaching in a nutshell.

a: See that I am buried well
p: Like Jacob and Joseph, Tobit's first request is for a proper burial, and for his wife's beside him.
b: Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him with his fathers (Genesis 47:29–30), and Joseph asks for his bones to be carried home (Genesis 50:25). Tobit, who risked his life burying others, asks the same for himself and for Anna "beside me in the same grave" (4:4). Tobias's fear in 6:15 is exactly that no son will be left to do it. He keeps the charge in 14:11–13.

a: Honor your mother
p: Tobit applies "Honor your father and your mother" to a widow's son: never leave her alone.
b: The commandment is "Honor your father and your mother, so that your days will stretch out long" (Exodus 20:12). Tobit spells out what it means once the father is gone: do not abandon her, do what makes her glad, do not grieve her. Sirach 3:1–16 is a longer sermon on the same command, and Jesus defends it against those who excuse themselves from supporting parents (Mark 7:10–13).

a: she faced many dangers for you while you were in her womb
p: Sirach gives the same reason to honor a mother: remember the pain she bore for you.
b: Sirach 7:27–28 says, in effect, "do not forget your mother's birth pangs; remember that you were born of your parents." In the ancient world childbirth was the most common danger to a young woman's life. Tobit asks his son to repay that risk with lifelong care.

a: For those who act in truth will succeed in what they do
p: To "do the truth" means to live faithfully. John's Gospel uses the same phrase.
b: The Greek poiein alētheian, "to do the truth," is a Hebrew way of speaking: truth is something you do, not only say. Jesus says, "the one who practices the truth comes to the light" (John 3:21), where "practices the truth" is the same Greek phrase, and 1 John 1:6 uses it too. Here, at the very point where Sinaiticus breaks off, the promise is that faithful living prospers, a theme from Psalm 1:3 and Joshua 1:8.

a: with a grudging eye
p: "Do not let your eye envy" is a Hebrew way of saying "do not be stingy".
b: In Hebrew idiom an "evil eye" is stinginess and a "good eye" generosity. Deuteronomy warns against an eye that is "evil" toward a poor brother (Deuteronomy 15:9), Proverbs speaks of the stingy man as "evil of eye" (Proverbs 23:6; Proverbs 28:22), and Jesus' "Is your eye evil because I am good?" (Matthew 20:15) means "Are you envious because I am generous?" The same idiom probably lies behind Matthew 6:22–23, set right after Jesus' teaching on treasure.
orig: μὴ φθονεσάτω σου ὁ ὀφθαλμὸς (mē phthonesatō sou ho ophthalmos), 'let not your eye envy'

a: Never turn your face from someone who is poor; then God will never turn his face from you
p: How we treat the poor is how God will treat us: an idea found in Proverbs and in Jesus' teaching.
b: Proverbs says, "Showing kindness to a poor man is a loan made to the LORD" (Proverbs 19:17), and "Plug your ears to a poor man's cry, and when you yourself cry out, no one will answer" (Proverbs 21:13). Jesus teaches the same pattern: "If someone asks you for something, give it" (Matthew 5:42) and "the measure you use is the one that will be used to measure out to you" (Luke 6:38). For God to "turn his face away" is to refuse to hear prayer (Psalm 27:9).

a: If you have only a little, do not be afraid to give alms in keeping with that little
p: The gift is measured by what one has. Paul and the story of the widow's coins say the same.
b: Paul writes that a gift is "measured by what a person has, not by what he lacks" (2 Corinthians 8:12), and Jesus praises the widow who put in two small coins (Mark 12:41–44). Tobit's words were spoken to a family that had just become poor (4:21).

a: a good deposit
p: Alms are a savings account with God for the day of need. Jesus speaks of treasure in heaven.
b: The Greek thema is a deposit placed for safekeeping, the same idea as Tobit's silver left with Gabael (1:14). Sirach 29:11–12 says, "lay up your treasure... it will rescue you from every disaster." Jesus tells his followers to "pile up treasures for yourselves in heaven" (Matthew 6:20) and to "Sell your property and give alms," making "an endless treasure in the heavens" (Luke 12:33). 1 Timothy 6:19 says generous people lay away "a fine foundation for what is coming." Whether the "day of need" means trouble in this life or the final judgment is part of the debate at 4:10.
orig: θέμα γὰρ ἀγαθὸν (thema gar agathon)

a: For alms rescue from death
p: Tobit's best-known saying. It reworks Proverbs' "righteousness rescues from death". Churches read it differently.
b: Proverbs 10:2 and 11:4 say "righteousness (tsedaqah) rescues from death." By Tobit's time tsedaqah also meant charity, and Tobit (with Sirach 3:30, "almsgiving atones for sins") reads the proverb that way; 12:9 goes further: alms "purge every sin." Agrees with Daniel 4:27 (break off your sins by mercy to the poor) and with Jesus' praise of almsgiving (Luke 11:41; Luke 12:33). Early Christian writers quoted it: Polycarp, in the early 100s, writes "almsgiving frees from death" (Philippians 10:2), and Cyprian builds a treatise on it. Goes beyond, as Protestants read it, if "death" means eternal death and alms are its remedy, since Christ alone frees from that (Romans 6:23). Many scholars think Tobit means an early or untimely death. See the card on this page.
r: Proverbs 10:2; Proverbs 11:4; Daniel 4:27; Luke 11:41; Luke 12:33; Romans 6:23; Sirach 3:30; 12:9

a: the darkness
p: The dark is the world of the dead, as in Job's "land of darkness". It is not clearly hell.
b: Job calls the realm of the dead "the land of darkness and deep shadow" (Job 10:21–22), and the psalmist asks, "Will the dark know your wonder" (Psalm 88:12). Tobit's "darkness" is most likely that world: alms keep a person from going down to it too soon. Christian readers have also heard the "outer darkness" of Jesus' parables (Matthew 8:12), but nothing in Tobit requires that sense.
orig: εἰς τὸ σκότος (eis to skotos)

a: their gift is a fine offering before the Most High
p: Giving to the poor is pictured as a sacrifice to God. The New Testament speaks the same way.
b: Sirach 35:2 says that one who gives alms offers a sacrifice of praise. Hebrews 13:16 says, "do not forget to do good and to share, for God is pleased with such sacrifices," and Paul calls a church's gift "a fragrant offering" (Philippians 4:18). The angel tells Cornelius, "Your prayers have gone up before God, and your alms too, as a remembrance" (Acts 10:4). For exiles far from the temple, alms were an offering they could still bring.

a: sexual immorality
p: Porneia covers every kind of sexual sin. Here it is closely tied to marrying outside one's people.
b: Porneia is the broad Greek word for sexual immorality (see Matthew 5:32; 1 Corinthians 6:18). In Tobit it leads straight into the command to marry within the family, and some Jewish writings of the time, such as Jubilees 30, treat marriage with Gentiles as a kind of defilement. The two ideas meet again in 8:7, where Tobias says he takes Sarah not out of lust.
orig: ἀπὸ πάσης πορνείας (apo pasēs porneias)

a: we are the sons of the prophets
p: Tobit calls Noah and the patriarchs prophets, as Genesis 20:7 and Psalm 105:15 do for Abraham's family.
b: God calls Abraham "a prophet" (Genesis 20:7), and Psalm 105:15 says of the patriarchs, "Don't hurt my prophets." 2 Peter 2:5 calls Noah "a herald of righteousness." Tobit's point is not a title but a family line: Israel descends from men who heard God, and their children should marry so as to keep that line.

a: all of them married women from among their own kin
p: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob did. Genesis never names Noah's wife; Tobit follows a tradition like Jubilees'.
b: Agrees: Abraham married Sarah, his half-sister (Genesis 20:12); he sent his servant to "go to my own land and my own relatives and take a wife for my son Isaac" (Genesis 24:4); and Jacob married his cousins (Genesis 28:2). Goes beyond: Genesis does not say whom Noah married; Jubilees 4:33 names her Emzara, daughter of his father's brother, and Tobit seems to know such a tradition. The 66 books forbid marriage with Canaanites and with worshipers of other gods (Deuteronomy 7:3–4; Ezra 10), but they also honor Joseph's Egyptian wife, Moses' Midianite wife and Ruth the Moabite. Only an heiress is told to marry within her tribe (Numbers 36:8). Tobit turns these into a general ideal for exiles.
r: Genesis 20:12; Genesis 24:3–4; Genesis 28:2; Deuteronomy 7:3–4; Numbers 36:8; Genesis 41:45; Ruth 4:13; Jubilees 4:33

a: idleness
p: The Greek achreotēs means uselessness or idleness. The KJV's "lewdness" misleads modern readers.
b: Achreotēs is "being of no use" (chrēsimos is "useful"). The point is that pride and laziness both lead to poverty: "idleness is the mother of hunger," a proverb close to Proverbs 6:9–11 and Proverbs 19:15. In 1611 "lewdness" could mean worthlessness or base conduct, but today it suggests sexual sin, which the Greek does not say.
orig: ἡ γὰρ ἀχρεότης μήτηρ ἐστὶν τοῦ λιμοῦ (hē gar achreotēs mētēr estin tou limou)

a: do not let his pay stay with you overnight
p: Tobit repeats the law: a hired worker's wages must not wait until morning.
b: Leviticus 19:13 says, "The wages of a hired worker must not stay with you overnight until morning," and Deuteronomy 24:15 adds, "Pay him his wages each day, before the sun goes down, because he is poor." The Greek verb here, aulisthētō, "let it not lodge overnight," matches the Greek of Leviticus. James 5:4 warns the rich whose withheld wages cry out to God, and in Jesus' parable the workers are paid at evening (Matthew 20:8).

a: Do not do to anyone what you hate
t: The Golden Rule, in its negative form
p: The oldest Jewish form of the Golden Rule. Hillel and the Didache give it the same way; Jesus states it positively.
b: Rabbi Hillel, about the time of Jesus, is said to have told a Gentile: "What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor; that is the whole law" (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a). The Didache 1:2 has the same negative form, and some manuscripts of Acts add it to the apostles' decree (Acts 15:20, 29, Codex Bezae). Jesus gives it positively: "whatever you want people to do to you, do the same to them" (Matthew 7:12; Luke 6:31). Both grow from "love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18).

a: Do not drink wine until you are drunk
p: Wine itself is not forbidden; drunkenness is, as in Proverbs and Ephesians.
b: Proverbs warns against those who linger over wine (Proverbs 23:20–21, 29–35), and Paul writes, "do not be drunk with wine" (Ephesians 5:18), using a Greek phrase close to Tobit's. Wine is served at the feasts in Tobit (7:14; 8:19) without blame.

a: Pour out your bread on the grave of the righteous
p: A puzzling command. It may mean feeding the mourners, or it may reflect the custom of food left at graves.
b: Readers take it three ways. (1) Feed the family of a righteous person who has died: mourners were brought "the bread of mourners" (Jeremiah 16:7; Ezekiel 24:17), and Tobit has just told his son to give his bread to the hungry (4:16). (2) A trace of the old custom of food offerings at tombs. The law has the worshiper declare, "I have not given any of it for the dead" (Deuteronomy 26:14), and Sirach 30:18 compares useless good things to food set on a grave. (3) Christian readers linked it to meals and alms in honor of the faithful dead: Augustine tells how his mother Monica brought bread and wine to the martyrs' shrines until Ambrose forbade the custom (Confessions 6.2). The Vulgate (4:18) reads "your bread and your wine."

a: For no nation has counsel
p: An awkward line in Vaticanus. Its point: true wisdom does not come from the nations but from God.
b: Word for word Vaticanus says "every nation does not have counsel" (the KJV keeps this: "every nation hath not counsel"). It probably means "no nation has counsel": wisdom does not belong to any people by nature, but the Lord himself gives every good thing, wisdom included. Proverbs says, "A person's heart is full of plans, but the LORD's purpose is the one that holds" (Proverbs 19:21), and James 1:5 tells anyone who lacks wisdom to ask God. Sinaiticus resumes here with "the Lord will give them good counsel"; the Plain does not join that clause to this one, because no manuscript has the two together (see the variants).
orig: πᾶν ἔθνος οὐκ ἔχει βουλήν (pan ethnos ouk echei boulēn)

a: Whomever the Lord wishes he brings low, down to the depths of Hades
t: God brings low and lifts up
p: Hannah's song says the same: the LORD brings down to Sheol and brings up.
b: Hannah sings, "The LORD kills and makes alive; he takes down to Sheol, and he brings up" (1 Samuel 2:6), and "he puts them down, and he also raises them up" (1 Samuel 2:7). Tobit's song repeats it (13:2). The words fit the whole book: Tobit is brought low almost to death and then raised up.

a: Many good things are yours if you fear God
p: Tobit ends where Proverbs does: the fear of God is worth more than money.
b: "A little, along with the fear of the LORD, is better than a big store of treasure with turmoil inside it" (Proverbs 15:16). 1 Timothy 6:6 says that godliness with contentment is great gain. Tobit's family has become poor, but he tells his son that the real inheritance is not the ten talents in Media.

a: I cut it in two, and each of us took one part
p: Ancient contracts were often written twice on one sheet and cut apart, so the halves could be matched.
b: Jeremiah's land deed was written in two copies, one sealed and one open (Jeremiah 32:10–14). Some ancient documents were written twice on one sheet and then cut, so that when the halves were brought together the cut and the writing would match. Tobias carries one half; Gabael's half proves the claim (9:5). Notice too that "twenty years" does not fit the book's own dates, since the deposit was made under Shalmaneser (1:14) and it is now Esarhaddon's reign; the story is not keeping a careful calendar.

a: Tobias had no idea that this was an angel of God
p: The reader knows; Tobias does not. The Bible has other angels who go unrecognized.
b: Abraham welcomes three strangers who turn out to be the LORD and two angels (Genesis 18–19). Of Samson's father we read, "Manoah did not know that this was the angel of the LORD" (Judges 13:16). Hebrews 13:2 says that some "have welcomed angels without knowing it," perhaps with stories like Tobit's in mind, and the disciples on the Emmaus road do not recognize the risen Jesus (Luke 24:16). The gap between what readers know and what Tobias knows runs through chapters 5–11 and gives them their humor and suspense.

a: a journey of two regular days
p: Rages is about 180 miles from Ecbatana, a journey of well over a week, and it is Ecbatana that lies high in the mountains.
b: Ecbatana (Hamadan) sits about 6,000 feet up in the Zagros mountains; Rages (near Tehran) lies at the foot of the Elburz range, at the edge of a plain, roughly 180 miles (300 km) away. The book's "two days" and its picture of Rages in the hills and Ecbatana on the plain are both mistaken. Most scholars conclude that the author did not know Media at first hand and wrote far away, perhaps in Syria-Palestine or Egypt. The Greek tetagmenōn means "set" or "regular": two standard days' stages. In Sinaiticus part of this sentence stands in the margin, but the first scribe seems simply to have skipped from one "Ecbatana" to the next, and the original corrector put the words back (see the variant), so the mistaken geography belongs to the text itself.

a: I am alive, yet I live among the dead
p: Tobit's blindness feels like being already in the grave, as the psalmist says of his suffering.
b: Psalm 88 says, "People already count me with those going down into the pit... turned loose among the dead" (Psalm 88:4–5), and Lamentations 3:6 says God "has made me live in dark places, like those long dead." In Tobit's world light is life: the healing he hopes for is "to see God's light" (3:17), and when he sees again he greets his son as the light of his eyes (11:14).

a: God is close to healing you
p: The one who says "God is close to healing you" is Raphael, whose name means "God heals".
b: Readers enjoy the double meaning. Raphael's promise is true in a way Tobit cannot guess: the healer God has sent is standing in front of him. The Greek engys para tō theō iasasthai se is literally "near with God is your healing."
orig: ἐγγὺς παρὰ τῷ θεῷ ἰάσασθαί σε (engys para tō theō iasasthai se)

a: Why do you need to know my tribe?
p: Raphael gives a human name and family (5:13). Readers have long asked whether an angel can deceive.
b: In 12:15 Raphael reveals who he really is. Before that, he calls himself Azariah son of Hananiah, a kinsman. Some interpreters call this a holy disguise like that of the angels with Abraham (Genesis 18) and note that the names fit his mission: Azariah means "the LORD helps" and Hananiah "the LORD is gracious." Others say plainly that the story lets the angel tell a white lie for a good end, as stories often do, and that the book is not interested in the question. Augustine held that no lie is ever right (On Lying), so readers in his tradition prefer the first answer. The question comes back when Raphael reveals himself; see the card "Can an angel deceive?" at Tobit 12.

a: Azariah, son of the great Hananiah
p: Hebrew names: Azariah, "the LORD has helped," and Hananiah, "the LORD has been gracious".
b: Azarias is the Greek form of Hebrew Azaryah, "the LORD helps," and Ananias of Hananyah, "the LORD is gracious." Both were common Jewish names; Daniel's friends bore them (Daniel 1:6–7). The Plain uses the Hebrew forms, Azariah and Hananiah, as English Bibles do in Daniel; the KJV of Tobit has Azarias and Ananias. Tobias calls his guide "Brother Azariah" (6:7).
orig: Ἀζαρίας Ἁνανίου τοῦ μεγάλου (Azarias Ananiou tou megalou)

a: a drachma a day
p: A drachma was a Greek silver coin, a day's pay. Coins like it did not exist in Assyria in the 700s BC.
b: The drachma was about a laborer's daily wage, like the Roman denarius in Jesus' parable (Matthew 20:2). Coined money began in Lydia in the 600s BC and the drachma spread with Greek trade and Alexander's conquests. A drachma in Nineveh is one more sign of the book's true date. Tobit's offer is generous: board as for his own son and a bonus (5:16).

a: May his angel go with you and keep you safe
p: Tobit's prayer echoes Abraham's blessing on the servant sent to find Isaac a wife: God will send his angel.
b: Abraham told his servant, "The LORD, in whose sight I have lived, will send his angel along with you and give you success on the road. You will take a wife for my son from my family and my father's house" (Genesis 24:40). Tobit's story follows the same pattern: a journey east, a wife from the family, an angel on the road. The irony is that the angel Tobit prays for is the young man he has just hired.

a: Let it count as rubbish next to our child
p: The Greek peripsēma means scrapings or refuse, and also a ransom given to avert evil.
b: Peripsēma is "what is wiped off": dirt, refuse. Paul uses it in "We have become like the scum of the world, the garbage of everything" (1 Corinthians 4:13). In Greek religion the word could also name a person or thing offered as a ransom to turn away disaster. So Anna may mean "money is rubbish compared with our son," or "let the money be a ransom for our son" (better to lose it than him). The first line is also hard: "let not money be added to money" or "let not money come first."
orig: περίψημα τοῦ παιδίου ἡμῶν (peripsēma tou paidiou hēmōn)

a: my sister
p: Husbands in Tobit call their wives "sister", as the lover does in the Song of Songs.
b: "My sister, my bride" is the lover's name for his beloved in the Song of Songs (Song of Songs 4:9–12). In Tobit Tobias calls Sarah "sister" in his wedding prayer (8:4, 7), and Raguel and Edna use the same family words (7:11–12). In a book that prizes marriage within the family, the word is also literal: husband and wife are kin.

a: For a good angel will go with him
p: Tobit's hope rests on angels who guard travelers. The 66 books promise the same; Tobit pictures it in a person.
b: Agrees: God promises Israel, "Here, I am sending an angel in front of you to keep you safe on the way" (Exodus 23:20). The psalms say God "will give his angels orders about you, to guard you on every road you take" (Psalm 91:11), and "The angel of the LORD pitches camp around those who fear him" (Psalm 34:7). Jesus speaks of the little ones' angels who see the Father's face (Matthew 18:10), and the believers in Acts 12:15 say, "It is his angel." Goes beyond: Tobit shows one named angel traveling as a companion for weeks, in human form; Jewish and Christian ideas of a personal guardian angel drew heavily on this story. See the card on this page.
r: Exodus 23:20; Psalm 91:11; Psalm 34:7; Matthew 18:10; Acts 12:15; Hebrews 1:14

a: The dog came out with him too
p: A pet dog is rare in Jewish writings, where dogs are usually scavengers. It returns in 11:4.
b: In the Hebrew Bible dogs are wild scavengers and "dog" is an insult (1 Samuel 17:43; 2 Kings 9:36; Psalm 22:16), though Job 30:1 mentions sheepdogs. A boy's dog trotting along on a journey stands out. Some scholars connect it with Persian religion, in which the dog is honored, or with Greek stories such as Odysseus's faithful dog in Homer's Odyssey 17; others see simply a homely detail. The dog runs ahead on the way home in 11:4.

a: A big fish jumped out of the water
p: In Christian art Tobias holding the fish, walking with Raphael, became a favorite picture of God's protection.
b: Painters of the Renaissance often showed a young Tobias carrying the fish and walking hand in hand with Raphael, among them Verrocchio's workshop in Florence (about 1470–1480). Such pictures were often given for sons setting off on journeys. Some early Christian readers saw in the fish a figure of Christ (the Greek ichthys, "fish," was read as an acrostic for "Jesus Christ, God's Son, Savior"), but nothing in Tobit points that way. In the story the fish is a danger turned into a gift.

a: This fish's gall, heart and liver make good medicine
p: Ancient doctors used fish gall for eye diseases. Smoke to drive away demons was common in Mesopotamian rites.
b: Pliny the Elder, in his Natural History (book 32), recommends the gall of certain fish for eye problems, including scars on the eye; so Raphael's remedy for Tobit's white films is the kind ancient doctors used. Burning substances to drive off evil spirits was common in Babylonian and Assyrian healing rites, and Josephus tells of a Jewish exorcist named Eleazar who drew out a demon with a root (Antiquities 8.45–49). Tobit's point is that the cure, whatever its means, comes from God through his angel.

a: attacked by a demon or an evil spirit
p: Tobit uses the same two words the Gospels use: daimonion, "demon", and pneuma ponēron, "evil spirit".
b: Daimonion and pneuma ponēron are the words of Luke 7:21 and Luke 8:2. The thing that attacks is an apantēma, literally a "meeting" or encounter, a word for a hostile run-in. Tobit's demon is not an "evil spirit from God" like Saul's (1 Samuel 16:14), but an enemy that God's angel defeats.
orig: ἀπάντημα δαιμονίου ἢ πνεύματος πονηροῦ (apantēma daimoniou ē pneumatos ponērou)

a: Make smoke from the fish's heart and liver
p: No book of the 66 drives out demons with a material remedy. Jesus does it with a word.
b: Goes beyond: in the Gospels Jesus drives out demons "with a word" (Matthew 8:16; Mark 1:25), and his followers do it in his name (Luke 10:17; Acts 16:18); no one uses smoke or herbs. Some Protestant readers have seen magic here and a reason to doubt the book. Catholic and Orthodox readers answer that the power is God's, carried by his angel, and the fish is only the means; in 8:3 it is Raphael who binds the demon, and Tobias and Sarah pray (8:4–8). Compare Jesus' use of mud and saliva to heal the blind (John 9:6; Mark 8:23), a material means for a healing that is God's work. See the card on this page.
r: Matthew 8:16; Mark 1:25; Luke 10:17; Acts 16:18; John 9:6; Mark 8:23; 8:2–3

a: Blow on the films, and the eyes will become well
p: The gall and the breath anticipate Tobit's healing (11:11–13) and recall Jesus' healings of the blind.
b: When Jesus healed a blind man at Bethsaida, he spat on his eyes and laid hands on him, and the man saw first "people... like trees, walking" (Mark 8:23–25). At Siloam he made mud and anointed the eyes (John 9:6–7). In Tobit the son, taught by the angel, heals the father (11:11–13).

a: You are her closest kinsman
p: Like Boaz in Ruth, the closest relative has the first right and duty to marry the heiress.
b: In Ruth a nearer kinsman must first refuse before Boaz can marry Ruth and redeem the land (Ruth 3:12–13; Ruth 4:4–6). Tobit applies a similar rule to Sarah: as the nearest eligible relative, Tobias has the first claim. Combined with the heiress law of Numbers 36, the result is a strong duty on both families.

a: The girl is sensible, brave and very beautiful
p: The Greek andreios usually means "manly, courageous". The Greek of Proverbs 31:10 uses it for the capable wife.
b: Andreios is unusual praise for a young woman. The Septuagint of Proverbs 31:10 uses the same word for the "capable wife" (Hebrew eshet chayil, "woman of strength"). Raphael's praise prepares the reader for a heroine who has already shown courage in choosing prayer over despair (3:10–15).
orig: φρόνιμον καὶ ἀνδρεῖον καὶ καλὸν λίαν (phronimon kai andreion kai kalon lian)

a: He would deserve death under the ruling of the book of Moses
p: No law of Moses puts a father to death for marrying his daughter outside the family.
b: Goes beyond: Numbers 36:6–9 tells heiresses to marry within their father's tribe, but sets no penalty, and nothing in the law orders the death of a father who gives his daughter to someone else. Scholars suggest the author is exaggerating Raphael's argument, reflecting a later custom, or applying the general curse on breaking the law (Deuteronomy 27:26). The book's readers would hear the point: the family duty to Tobias is serious.

a: The demon does not harm her, but he kills anyone who wants to come near her
p: Vaticanus says the demon "loves her". Readers have seen jealousy, the danger of a wedding night, or a test of trust.
b: In Vaticanus Tobias says plainly that "a demon loves her", so many readers take Asmodeus as a jealous lover, like the Watchers who desired human women (Genesis 6:2; 1 Enoch 6–7). Others note that in the ancient world the wedding night was a time of special danger from spirits. The Vulgate (6:16–17) turns it into a moral lesson: the devil has power over those who marry "to shut out God" and serve lust. Raphael's answer in the Greek is simpler: obey your father, pray, and do not fear.

a: the two of you must first get up and pray
p: Raphael tells the couple to pray before they come together. The Vulgate turns this into three nights of prayer.
b: The Greek has a single prayer before the couple come together, which Tobias and Sarah pray in 8:4–8. Jerome's Latin (6:18–22) gives Raphael a longer speech: Tobias is to keep himself from Sarah for three nights and pray, so that on the third night they will be blessed with children, and to take her "moved rather for love of children than for lust." Through the Vulgate this became a Catholic custom of prayer and restraint at the start of marriage, sometimes called the "Tobias nights," and the Latin passage shaped medieval teaching on marriage. Christian readers paired it with Paul's advice that a married couple may abstain for a time by agreement, to give themselves to prayer (1 Corinthians 7:5). See the variant on this verse.

a: she was allotted to you before the ages
p: Raphael says Sarah was set aside for Tobias before time began. Jewish tradition says matches are made in heaven.
b: The verb memerismenē means "assigned as a share." Abraham's servant prays to find the one God "picked out for your servant Isaac" (Genesis 24:14), and the rabbis taught that forty days before a child is formed, a voice from heaven announces whom he will marry (Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 2a). Readers differ on whether this means fixed destiny or God's loving care that works through human choices; in Tobit, Tobias still has to choose, obey and pray.
orig: σοὶ γάρ ἐστιν μεμερισμένη πρὸ τοῦ αἰῶνος (soi gar estin memerismenē pro tou aiōnos)

a: his heart clung to her
p: The verb is the one Genesis 2:24 uses for a man joining his wife.
b: The Greek ekollēthē, "was glued, clung," shares its root with the Septuagint's verb in Genesis 2:24 (proskollēthēsetai), where a man "sticks close to his wife, and they become one flesh." Tobias loves Sarah before he has met her, because of what he has heard of her, and because she is of his own family.
orig: ἡ καρδία αὐτοῦ ἐκολλήθη εἰς αὐτήν (hē kardia autou ekollēthē eis autēn)
